To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

HIV-2 protease sequences from India are closely related to HIV subtype A sequences from West Africa and that HIV-2 RT sequences from India are more closely related to HIV 2 subtype A2 than subtype A1.

the sequences from HIV-2-infected treatment-naïve individuals from India are closely related to those from Guinea-Bissau, and two unique residues were identified in the protease region, as well as drug resistance mutations in 3 of the 32 samples.

the sequences from Indian HIV-2 subtype B infected individuals were closely related to those from Guinea Bissausubtype A, and that the mutations associated with resistance to protease inhibitors were not observed.

the identification and characterization of the genetic variation of HIV-2 pol sequences in Indian population.
the study of the genetic diversity of HIV-2 in Maharashtra, India and the potential for the emergence of antiretrovirus resistance.
the identification of the HIV-2 subtype in India and to determine the drug resistance profile of treatment-naïve patients.

this study has provided an insight into the genetic diversity and drug resistance in HIV-2 infected patients from Maharashtra, India.
this study is a step towards understanding the HIV-2 subtype distribution and the drug resistance profile in the Indian population.
the Indian HIV-2 sequences are closely related to the West African HIV-2 subtype and the drug resistance among the treatment naive individuals is low in this region.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

this study reports the sequence data of PR and RT genes from HIV-1 naive individuals from Maharashtra, India and highlights the need of larger nationwide surveillance for drug resistance among HIV infected individuals.
this is the first Indian report of drug resistance among HIV 2 infected treatment naive patients.
we have reported the first study on HIV-2 protease and reverse transcriptase sequences from treatment naive individuals in India.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HIV-2 subtype in India is closely related to the subtype in Guinea Bissau and that the HIV-1 subtype C is the predominant subtype in India.
there are unique HIV-2 sequences in India, and that the HIV-2 sequences are not as well studied in India as the HIV-1 sequences.
the HIV-2 subtype in India is closely related to the West African HIV-2 subtypes and is not yet resistant to the first-line drugs used for treatment of HIV-2.
